name: Sara Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a farm hand on the Ashby Estate, which is big, about two thousand acres of wheat and oilseed and twelve hundred ewes. It depends on the season: lambing in March means nights in the shed, harvest means carting grain in a tractor that more or less steers itself, and the rest is fencing, shepherding and moving sheep with the quad. Graham Doyle, the farm manager, gives out the jobs at seven in the yard office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it, and how are you finding it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a cook in a school canteen for fifteen years, and when they brought in the outside catering firm I took the redundancy. A friend said the estate needed help at lambing, and I stayed. It's two years now and I'm still the one Graham sends to do the simple jobs, which is fair, I'm learning. My husband Luis works the counter at the builders' merchant, we've got Mateo who's thirteen and Carla who's nine, and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a lot of noise and not much change. At work the lads would laugh about it. I might share a meme about it on the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays my job, but my job's not that secure anyway. The estate cut winter overtime last year, and that was my extra money. We've got about two months saved, maybe three, which isn't much with two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Graham for more shifts in the busy months. I'd pick up a Saturday cooking shift at the café in the village, which I've done before. Nothing more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the money, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a tractor that more or less steers itself. How do you feel about that already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tractor on the Ashby Estate already steers itself down the field; all I do is turn it round at the end and watch the screen. I didn't mind, it's easier on my back. But it makes you think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you now, before any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The overtime. Graham said the estate's watching costs, and I'm the newest. If they cut one hand, it'd be me.

I might share a **meme** about it on the family group chat.
think: My job stays, but it's **not that secure** anyway.

do: Ask Graham for **more shifts** in the busy months.
Pick up a **Saturday cooking** shift at the village café.

fieldNote: Her worry is the **lost overtime** and being the newest hand.

Falls back on her old trade, **cooking**, for extra money.

steps.text: Ask Graham for extra shifts at lambing and harvest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll take some getting used to, but people will manage. At work I'd say the estate will try things first, it always does. Online I'd stay out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think both of us feel it. Luis does orders and answers customers all day, and that's on the list for the first wave. On the estate, Graham's ordering and planning gets done by software, and then he's got more time to look at what else can be automated, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the sprayer ticket this spring, because the estate needs qualified people for that and it's paid better. I'd learn whatever the estate's new app is, once the others have figured it out. And I'd put an extra hundred a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Luis works the counter at the builders' merchant. Does this picture touch his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband takes orders and answers customers all day at the builders' merchant, and that's exactly the work this picture says goes first. He says they'll always need someone to find the right screws. I hope he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then, to check a sheep drench dose or to help Mateo with homework. I'd use it more if Graham set it up. I'm not the first to try things, but I don't run away from them.

fieldNote: She sees a **two-income risk**: Luis's counter job and her own junior role.
A **steady adopter**, she'd learn tools once proven by others.
Plans a qualification, the **sprayer ticket**, to be harder to cut.

steps.text: Take the sprayer qualification this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and somebody should slow it down. At work I'd say we need to know what the estate plans. Online I'd probably share petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I lose my job, simple as that. Luis's counter job goes in 2028, and on a big estate with money, robots will be doing shepherding and fencing by 2031. I'm junior, I'm the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd cut everything we don't need, the holiday, the second car. I'd look at retraining in something that's people-facing, maybe care work, because I know canteen work is gone. And I'd lean on my mum, who's offered to help with the kids if I work longer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's keeping me awake just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots by 2031 on an estate like Ashby. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate's got the money to buy the first robots in the county. A big estate with money will have robot shepherds before the small farms have even heard of them. Graham would keep the best hands for supervising, and I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Carla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a team and we'll get through it, but they might have to give up some things. Mateo would sulk about the football club. Carla would want to know if she still gets her birthday party.

think: Luis's job goes in **2028**, and robots do shepherding and fencing by **2031**.

feel: **Alarmed**, kept awake just thinking about it.
S2.quote: A big estate with money will have robot shepherds before the small farms have even heard of them.
fieldNote: She expects **both incomes** to go within three years.
Sees the rich estate as an **early adopter** of robots.

steps.text: Cancel the family holiday and sell the second car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it right, if people want to. At work I'd be asking Graham what training the estate will pay for. I'd stay quiet online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got until about 2034 before the robots catch up on the hands-on work. Luis's counter job probably goes by 2031. That's time to get a qualification and save a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sprayer ticket and then a machinery maintenance course over two years. I'd save two hundred a month. And I'd help Luis look for something new early, before the merchant cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Better than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, what's different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, I like the sheep and the open air. If someone has to look after the robots that look after the sheep, I'd like that someone to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in farming if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I'd keep the care work idea as a backup. Two years of training is two years, either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, so there's no excuse for anybody. I'd still ask Graham about training. Maybe I'd post something hopeful for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd likely be fine if I use the time. I'd be fifty-six by 2039, the mortgage mostly paid, the kids grown. Luis would have years to change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sprayer ticket, then the maintenance course, at a steady pace. I'd learn the estate's software as it comes. And I'd keep working, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe. It's there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to learn a new trade and still be useful. Two years isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'd like to be the person Graham (the farm manager) calls when a machine on the Ashby Estate breaks down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Luis would lose his counter job first, and then me three years later, and we'd have two months saved and two kids. What would help is training that's paid for and that you can do while you're still working. Nobody on a farm wage can afford to stop earning for two years to learn the next job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the animals. I don't know if a robot can tell when a ewe is about to have trouble. I'd like to know that somebody's thought about it.

She already drives a **self-steering tractor** and knows the estate adopts machines early.
Her husband Luis's **counter job** is exposed to the first wave of thinking AI.
She is a **steady adopter**, planning sprayer and maintenance tickets.
She is **alarmed** by AGI by 2028 and uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when Luis's job and hers could go within three years.
